title: Israel's deadlocked election
deck: Israel votes on 27 October in a referendum on Netanyahu's handling of Gaza and the Iran war, and the latest poll leaves both camps short of a majority.

card.headline: Israel votes on 27 October with neither camp near a majority, and the result will shape the Iran war

keyNumber.label: seats for Netanyahu's bloc vs the anti-Netanyahu bloc in a Kan poll on 18 October; 61 of 120 are needed

forYou.line: The result may decide whether the Iran war escalates. Brent is above $100 against $73 before the war, so a hawkish outcome keeps risk premiums high.
Expect a drawn-out coalition process rather than a clean result. Caretaker governments tend to avoid big decisions.
The cabinet has approved NIS 2.6 billion in cuts to fund defence. The next government inherits that choice.
Trump has endorsed Netanyahu. A narrow result could test how far that endorsement carries.

effects.text: A 120-seat Knesset is elected on 27 October, the first vote on the legally scheduled date since 1988
Kan poll of 18 October: Eisenkot's Yashar 23 seats, Likud 21; Netanyahu's bloc 51, anti-Netanyahu bloc 52
Trump's endorsement of Netanyahu and the NIS 2.6 billion defence-funding cuts become campaign issues
A new far-right party polls under the threshold while Smotrich gains, per Haaretz's 18 October poll report
With neither bloc at 61, coalition talks could run for weeks, and the Arab parties may become kingmakers
A caretaker government limits major budget and policy moves during talks
Votes for parties below the threshold are wasted, which can shift the final seat count by a few seats

whatHappened: Israel elects its 120-seat Knesset on 27 October 2026. It is the first election held on its legally scheduled date since 1988.

A Kan poll on 18 October put Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar first with 23 seats, ahead of Likud with 21. It gave Netanyahu's bloc 51 seats and the anti-Netanyahu bloc 52, counting the Arab parties separately. Neither camp reaches the 61 seats needed to govern.

Haaretz reported the same day that a new far-right party is polling below the electoral threshold while Smotrich is gaining. Trump has endorsed Netanyahu, and the cabinet has approved NIS 2.6 billion in cuts to pay for defence.
whyItMatters: The campaign is a referendum on Netanyahu's handling of Gaza and the US-Israel war on Iran. Netanyahu vows to topple Tehran's regime. The strikes began on 27 February 2026 and have kept oil and freight costs high for eight months.
Whether the war escalates or cools affects Gulf export capacity. Gulf exports through Hormuz are running at roughly 60 to 80% of normal, and Brent is above $100. OPEC+ meets again on 1 November.
A deadlock could leave Israel with weeks of coalition bargaining. Nobody would then have a clear mandate on war aims, defence spending or the US relationship.

winners.why: They lead the 18 October Kan poll by two seats, which is within normal polling error.
Haaretz's poll report says he is gaining, partly as a new far-right rival falls below the threshold.
If both blocs stay short of 61, small parties and possibly the Arab parties gain bargaining power.

losers.why: His bloc is at 51 in the poll, ten short of a majority, and Likud trails Yashar by two seats.
Polling under the threshold would leave it with no seats, and its voters' ballots would be wasted.

losers.who: Public services and budget lines outside defence
losers.why: The NIS 2.6 billion cuts fund defence. Our material does not say which areas are cut.

whatsNext: Within roughly a week: certified results, after which Israel's president consults the parties and picks someone to try to form a government. The legal timetable is about four weeks plus a possible extension, from general knowledge.
1 November: OPEC+ core producers meet, with the Gulf war's direction still unresolved.
Late 2026: either a coalition forms, or talks drag on or fail, which could mean another election.

predict.question: Before you read the scenarios: what is the most likely result on 27 October?
options: The anti-Netanyahu bloc wins 61 seats without the Arab parties
Neither bloc reaches 61 and coalition talks run long
A national unity government forms within days
predict.explanation: Our base case, at about 40%, is deadlock. The Kan poll leaves both blocs far from 61, and the gap would take a large swing to close. This is author judgement from one poll.

timeline.title: Last election held on its scheduled date
timeline.detail: Israel's 1988 vote was the last one held on schedule until now. A Likud-Labor national unity government followed (general knowledge).

timeline.title: US and Israeli strikes on Iran begin
timeline.detail: Oil and freight costs stay elevated for months afterwards. The war becomes the central issue in the campaign.

timeline.title: OPEC+ holds November output targets
timeline.detail: Gulf exports through Hormuz are running at roughly 60 to 80% of normal, and Brent is above $100.

timeline.title: Library of Congress publishes an explainer on the vote
timeline.detail: The FALQs piece sets out how the 27 October election works.

timeline.title: Kan poll puts Yashar first
timeline.detail: Yashar 23, Likud 21; Netanyahu's bloc 51, anti-Netanyahu bloc 52. Haaretz reports a new far-right party below the threshold and Smotrich gaining.

timeline.title: OPEC+ core producers meet again
timeline.detail: The meeting follows the Israeli vote, with the Iran war's direction unresolved.

causes.name: Proportional system with a low threshold
causes.detail: Many parties compete, and a bloc needs 61 of 120 seats. The threshold is 3.25% from general knowledge, so some parties can win just a few seats and others can fall short.

causes.name: Two evenly matched blocs
causes.detail: The poll shows 51 against 52, so a few seats or a few wasted votes can decide who governs.

causes.name: Netanyahu as the dividing line
causes.detail: Politics is organised around being for or against him, which makes cross-bloc deals harder.

causes.name: End of the legal term
causes.detail: The election is held on its legally scheduled date, not after an early collapse, for the first time since 1988.

causes.name: Iran war
causes.detail: Strikes began on 27 February. Netanyahu vows to topple Tehran's regime, and the vote is framed as a referendum on this.

causes.name: Gaza
causes.detail: The campaign is also a judgement on how the Gaza war was handled.

causes.name: Defence-funding cuts
causes.detail: The cabinet approved NIS 2.6 billion in cuts to fund defence, which makes budget priorities a campaign issue.

causes.name: Trump's endorsement
causes.detail: It strengthens Netanyahu with some voters and may harden opposition among others.

causes.name: Far-right vote split
causes.detail: A new far-right party sinks under the threshold while Smotrich gains, so the right's votes may be partly wasted.

stakeholders.name: Benjamin Netanyahu
stakeholders.wants: A bloc majority and a mandate to continue the Iran war and defence build-up
stakeholders.leverage: Incumbency, the Trump endorsement, and a Likud that polls close to the leader
stakeholders.likelyMove: Frame the vote as a choice on Iran and security, and court small right-wing parties

stakeholders.name: Gadi Eisenkot
stakeholders.wants: To become prime minister and move the country away from the current leadership
stakeholders.leverage: A two-seat poll lead over Likud, and a bloc just ahead of Netanyahu's
stakeholders.likelyMove: Stress security credentials and seek a broad coalition, possibly including Arab parties or defectors

stakeholders.name: Bezalel Smotrich
stakeholders.wants: To survive and keep influence over the next coalition and its budget
stakeholders.leverage: Seats that could tip a right-wing majority, and gains reported by Haaretz
stakeholders.likelyMove: Absorb voters from the failing new far-right party and press for a hard line on security

stakeholders.name: Arab parties
stakeholders.role: Outside both blocs in the Kan count
stakeholders.wants: Policy influence and a role in a post-Netanyahu majority
stakeholders.leverage: If the anti-Netanyahu bloc stays at about 52, their seats could decide who reaches 61
stakeholders.likelyMove: Stay out of formal coalitions but signal conditional support, though this is our judgement

stakeholders.name: Israel's president
stakeholders.role: Chooses who tries to form a government
stakeholders.wants: A functioning government within the legal deadlines
stakeholders.leverage: The power to pick which party leader gets the first attempt
stakeholders.likelyMove: Hold consultations after certified results and pick whoever shows the strongest backing

stakeholders.name: Donald Trump
stakeholders.wants: A partner for the Iran campaign and a sympathetic government in Jerusalem
stakeholders.leverage: Public endorsement and US military and diplomatic backing
stakeholders.likelyMove: Keep backing Netanyahu publicly, and deal with whoever wins if the result is close

sectors.why: The result may decide how far the Iran war escalates. Brent is above $100 against $73 before the war.
The NIS 2.6 billion in cuts to fund defence signals priority, whichever bloc governs.
The cuts fund defence. Which services bear them is not specified in our material.
Deadlock and caretaker rule can delay budgets and decisions. This is an estimate, not a sourced finding.
Gulf powers compete for Red Sea positions while Washington's attention is on Iran.

dailyLife.effect: Brent is above $100 against $73 before the war. French diesel hit a record EUR 2.41 a litre in September.
Elevated for eight months because of the Iran war and attacks on Gulf infrastructure.
The NIS 2.6 billion in cuts will fall somewhere in public spending, though the details are not in our sources.
Expect heavy news flow, and then days or weeks of coalition headlines rather than an instant outcome.

scenarios.name: Deadlock and long coalition talks
scenarios.looksLike: Neither bloc reaches 61. The president tasks someone, talks run to the legal limit, and a caretaker government stays in place.
signposts: Final results near the 18 October poll
Both leaders ruling out deals with the other side
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Iran war policy stays unchanged by default, and Gulf and OPEC+ planning stays uncertain.

scenarios.name: Anti-Netanyahu government forms
scenarios.looksLike: Eisenkot assembles 61 seats with outside support or defectors from the Netanyahu bloc.
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Possible change in Iran war tactics. Washington would have to deal with a new prime minister after endorsing Netanyahu.

scenarios.name: Netanyahu keeps power
scenarios.looksLike: Wasted votes below the threshold and a polling miss lift the bloc to 61, or enough rivals defect to him.
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Iran regime-change rhetoric continues, with continued high oil risk premiums.

scenarios.name: Cross-bloc unity government
scenarios.looksLike: Both big parties agree to share power to avoid another election.
signposts: Netanyahu stepping back from the leadership of Likud
Public talk of unity from Yashar and Likud
scenarios.effectOnWorld: A more stable but cautious government, with less certainty on Iran policy.

predictions.text: Neither bloc will hold 61 seats on certified results (probability 0.8).
Yashar will win more seats than Likud (probability 0.5, since a two-seat lead is within polling error).
No new government will be sworn in by the end of 2026 (probability 0.55).
Netanyahu will still be prime minister, including as caretaker, on 31 December 2026 (probability 0.75).
The vote will not produce an Iran ceasefire by the end of November (probability 0.8).

actions: Plan for weeks of political uncertainty rather than a clean result.
Keep fuel and freight surcharges in contracts while Brent is above $100.
Avoid committing to Israeli government contracts that depend on a new budget until a government forms.
Do not assume the election resolves Iran war risk; treat the result as one input.
Watch the 1 November OPEC+ meeting alongside Israeli coalition headlines.
Treat polls as uncertain: a two-seat lead is within normal error.
Expect fuel and food prices to stay high while the Gulf war continues.
Do not expect an immediate change in policy after election day.
Prepare for several possible coalitions, including a drawn-out caretaker period.
Clarify to partners what US backing means whichever bloc wins.
Coordinate Gulf and Red Sea contingency planning, since attention is concentrated on Iran.

analogues.event: Israel's five elections in under four years
analogues.whatFollowed: Repeated deadlock ended in the Bennett-Lapid coalition, which included an Arab party and collapsed within a year. Netanyahu returned to power after the November 2022 vote.
Kadima won the most seats, but Netanyahu formed the government, showing the largest party does not always govern.
A Likud-Labor national unity government formed, an example of cross-bloc power sharing after a close vote.

watch.title: Election day
watch.why: The first scheduled vote since 1988, with the blocs at 51 and 52 in the last poll.

watch.title: OPEC+ core producers' meeting
watch.why: It is the next signal on whether Gulf export capacity is returning, and the Iran war's direction feeds into it.

watch.title: Final-week polls
watch.why: Israel restricts poll publication in the final days before the vote (general knowledge), so late shifts may be hard to see.

watch.title: Far-right parties and the threshold
watch.why: Whether the new far-right party falls below it or Smotrich gains changes which bloc has the better path to 61.

watch.title: Presidential consultations
watch.why: Who is asked to form a government will show which coalition path looks most credible.

watch.title: Ethiopia-Eritrea at the UN Security Council
watch.why: A parallel Red Sea dispute in which Gulf powers are involved while Washington is distracted by Iran.

evidence.method: Drafted from the two listed sources, which were available as headlines and metadata only, the event summary, and the supplied notes on connected events. No article text was read. The seat figures come from the summary. The probabilities, the interpretation of the blocs and Arab parties, and the general-knowledge details on thresholds and coalition timing are estimates and are flagged as such in the text and in the confidence entries.
